Server Administration Guide, "Managing organizations": "In the Organizations section, you can manage all the organizations in your realm. Creating an organization: Click Create Organization. An organization has the following settings: Name — a user-friendly name for the organization. The name is unique within a realm."

Server Administration Guide documents "W3C Web Authentication (WebAuthn)" setup ("Enable WebAuthn authentication in the default browser flow", "WebAuthn together with Two-Factor", "LoginLess WebAuthn") and a dedicated "Passkeys" section: "Passkey Authentication with Conditional UI or autofill", "Passkeys Authentication with Modal UI", "Passkey Mediation".

Server Administration Guide, "Managing users and groups through SCIM": built-in SCIM endpoints per realm ("Enabling SCIM for a realm", "Obtaining the SCIM API base URL", "Setting up a service account client"), with protected admin users excluded: "resources can only be managed through the Admin Console or the Admin REST API, never through SCIM."

Server Administration Guide, "Device authorization grant": "This is used by clients running on internet-connected devices that have limited input capabilities or lack a suitable browser." The OIDC layers reference documents the endpoint: "/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/openid-connect/auth/device ... used to obtain a device code and a user code."

OIDC layers reference, "Client credentials": "Client Credentials are used when clients (applications and services) want to obtain access on behalf of themselves rather than on behalf of a user." Clients authenticate via client_id/client_secret or JWT, backing service accounts for machine-to-machine access.

Server Administration Guide documents the Admin CLI: Keycloak "packages the Admin CLI server distribution with the execution scripts in the bin directory. The Linux script is called kcadm.sh", enabling scripted administration of realms, users, roles, and clients; the same operations are available over the Admin REST API.

Server Administration Guide, brute force protection events: "User disabled by permanent lockout — Brute force protection disabled the user account permanently due to too many login failures. User disabled by temporary lockout — Brute force protection disabled the user account temporarily due to too many login failures."

Keycloak site, Identity Brokering and Social Login: "Enabling login with social networks is easy to add through the admin console. It's just a matter of selecting the social network you want to add. No code or changes to your application" — brokering also covers external OpenID Connect or SAML identity providers.

Keycloak site, User Federation: "Keycloak has built-in support to connect to existing LDAP or Active Directory servers. You can also implement your own provider if you have users in other stores, such as a relational database."

Authorization Services guide: fine-grained, resource-level authorization — "A resource is part of the assets of an application and the organization... In authorization policy terminology, a resource is the object being protected", with policies evaluated via UMA permission tickets and client-credentials-obtained PATs.

Startup tried Keycloak: it needed a lot of memory, was very slow to start, and the Docker images were huge. It also required Gatekeeper, which was later obsoleted. Community support was less active than other FOSS projects, so they ditched it for a proprietary auth solution.

Used for 6-7 years and very stable, running clustered without issues. They integrated many external IdPs for SSO across multiple software stacks. It helps that the team has a Java background and isn't worried about memory use.

Best treated as a 'pet' rather than 'cattle': it takes a while to warm up, so avoid constant restarts. Powerful, full-featured and configurable, but it doesn't play well with infrastructure-as-code. You can load a realm from JSON, but keeping later changes synced is hard.
Biggest complaint is poor documentation. You will need to set various flags for your use case, with lots of googling and Stack Overflow. Options changed since 17.x, so many guides are outdated.
One user dropped Keycloak because its 2 GiB of RAM was too much to commit to SSO on a tiny VPS, and switched to static htpasswd.
Uses Keycloak for all authentication, in the cloud on Linux and in Windows enterprise environments. Provides SSO for Node-RED, Grafana, ASP.NET and VueJS apps. Moving from Auth0 was fairly easy.

Nothing made sense until learning OAuth 2.0/OIDC. The docs seem vast but aren't and can't be searched; the admin UI tooltips help more. "It never failed for me," and upgrading from 7.x to 16.x just worked. The Docker image is still big at 562MB.

Works great but is hard to understand without OAuth/OIDC knowledge and is heavyweight. WildFly/Infinispan/Quarkus packaging means learning many dependencies, likely a serious admin burden if you don't already deploy Java apps.
In the evaluated version, Keycloak didn't make it easy to stop users changing their own email. With service providers that use email as the username, this makes impersonation trivial.
Great when authenticating against on-prem AD. It isolates messy OU and domain layouts behind a simple OAuth 2.0/OIDC interface.
"I've run keycloak securing internet facing apps with ~1000 users for years. It's so stable, I usually forget it's even there."
Loves Keycloak but is disappointed it can't act as an LDAP server for internal SSO. Had to rely on the more expensive GSuite Identity Premium instead.

Automating resources with Ansible is hard because the admin API is inconsistent. Some GETs return incomplete payloads, and some endpoints don't save on POST but do on update, making idempotency very hard.

After Okta told them, as paying customers, to pay extra or leave, they found Keycloak four years ago "and never looked back." They describe it as stable, customizable, well engineered and relatively easy to work with.

Feels like clunky 90s enterprise software. Running it on OpenShift was hell: not made for containers, clustering basically impossible, needs to know its default route. The user had to patch obscure startup scripts that template XML.

Used for auth and SSO across 10+ Java services with a custom UI and 2FA. LDAP setup was easy, Google SSO was a few settings away, and it ran on Docker without problems. The admin UI was at times clunky, but the docs were good.

Configuration is stored in the database, so you can't define it in YAML or easily promote changes from test to production; you click around the UI. The third-party keycloak-config-cli helps but doesn't work as well as a first-party solution.

Production user misses opaque token support. After a login tab sits idle, the expired session isn't auto-refreshed, so users get an error and must re-authenticate. With two tabs, one shows 'already logged in' and loses the redirect URL.

Called "an amazing product" across many instances at work. But you can't easily add a custom page next to the login flow without extending Keycloak. New UI changes buried simple tasks like client role assignment behind multiple screens.

Running as an enterprise Java app means a steady stream of high/critical CVEs in bundled WildFly dependencies such as SnakeYAML, Apache SSHD, H2 and Infinispan, which you probably don't use but must patch.
